questions.prompt: How is unsold stock on consignment valued? Explain the treatment of normal and abnormal loss.
questions.answer:
- Unsold stock is valued at cost plus a proportionate share of non-recurring expenses incurred up to the point of bringing the goods to the consignee's godown (freight, insurance in transit, unloading, octroi). Recurring and selling expenses, and commission, are excluded.
- Per AS 2, it is shown at the lower of this cost and net realisable value.
- Normal loss is inherent (evaporation, drying). It is not recorded separately; the total cost is spread over the units remaining after normal loss, which raises the cost per unit of stock.
- Abnormal loss arises from accidents, theft or negligence. It is valued like stock, at cost plus proportionate non-recurring expenses up to the point of loss, credited to Consignment Account and debited to Abnormal Loss Account; after any insurance claim, the balance goes to P&L.

chapters.title: Final Accounts of Sole Proprietors and Not-for-Profit Organisations
chapters.summary: Trading, Profit and Loss Account and Balance Sheet with adjustments, and the Receipts and Payments, Income and Expenditure Account and Balance Sheet of not-for-profit organisations.

lesson.heading: Format of final accounts
lesson.body:
For a sole proprietor, final accounts are the **Trading Account** (gross profit), **Profit and Loss Account** (net profit) and **Balance Sheet** (financial position).

| Trading A/c debits | Trading A/c credits |
| --- | --- |
| Opening stock | Sales less returns inward |
| Purchases less returns outward and drawings of goods | Closing stock |
| Direct expenses: wages, carriage inwards, freight, factory power, import duty |  |
| Gross profit (balancing figure) |  |

P&L Account: gross profit, indirect expenses (salaries, rent, office and selling expenses, depreciation, bad debts, interest on loan) and other incomes. Net profit is added to capital; drawings are deducted.

Balance Sheet: capital and liabilities on one side, assets on the other, usually in order of permanence or liquidity.

lesson.heading: Adjustments and their double effect
lesson.body:
Every adjustment is recorded twice: once in Trading/P&L and once in the Balance Sheet.

| Adjustment | Trading / P&L | Balance Sheet |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Closing stock | Credit Trading A/c | Current asset |
| Outstanding expense | Add to expense | Current liability |
| Prepaid expense | Deduct from expense | Current asset |
| Accrued income | Add to income | Current asset |
| Income received in advance | Deduct from income | Current liability |
| Depreciation | Debit P&L | Deduct from asset |
| Further bad debts | Debit P&L | Deduct from debtors |
| Provision for doubtful debts | Debit P&L: bad debts + new provision - old provision | Deduct new provision from debtors |
| Goods withdrawn by owner | Deduct from purchases | Add to drawings |
| Interest on capital | Debit P&L | Add to capital |
| Interest on drawings | Credit P&L | Add to drawings |

Rule: an adjustment given **outside** the trial balance has two effects; an item **inside** the trial balance has only one (closing stock inside the trial balance appears only in the Balance Sheet).

Provision is computed on debtors **after** deducting further bad debts.

lesson.heading: Not-for-profit organisations
lesson.body:
Clubs, societies, charitable trusts and similar bodies exist to serve members, not to earn profit. They prepare:

- **Receipts and Payments Account**: summary of cash and bank; real account; starts with opening cash/bank, records all receipts and payments (capital or revenue, any year), ends with closing balance. No outstanding or non-cash items.
- **Income and Expenditure Account**: nominal account like P&L, on accrual basis, only revenue items of the current year. Excess of income over expenditure is a **surplus**; the reverse is a **deficit**.
- **Balance Sheet**: the **Capital Fund** (General / Accumulated Fund) replaces capital. Opening Capital Fund = opening assets - opening liabilities.

Special items:

- **Subscriptions** (income for the year) = Received - for previous year - for next year + outstanding at end + received in advance last year for this year.
- **Legacies**: capitalised (added to Capital Fund).
- **Specific donations** (building fund) and **special funds**: liabilities; expenses on them are deducted from the fund, not shown in I&E.
- **General donations**: usually revenue income unless large and specifically treated as capital.
- **Entrance and life membership fees**: follow the organisation's policy; life membership is normally capitalised.
- **Sale of old assets**: only profit or loss goes to I&E.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
Subscriptions received in 2026-27 ₹2,40,000 include ₹18,000 for 2025-26 and ₹12,000 for 2027-28. Subscriptions outstanding for 2026-27 at year end ₹22,000; received in 2025-26 in advance for 2026-27 ₹9,000.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Subscriptions received | 2,40,000 |
| Less: For 2025-26 | (18,000) |
| Less: For 2027-28 (advance) | (12,000) |
| Add: Outstanding for 2026-27 | 22,000 |
| Add: Received last year for 2026-27 | 9,000 |
| **Income for 2026-27** | **2,41,000** |

**Common mistakes**: computing provision before deducting further bad debts; putting closing stock given inside the trial balance in the Trading Account; showing legacies or specific donations as income; including outstanding subscriptions in Receipts and Payments.

keyPoints: Items outside the trial balance (adjustments) have two effects; items inside have one.
P&L charge for bad debts = bad debts (incl. further) + new provision - old provision.
Goods withdrawn by the owner: deduct from purchases at cost, add to drawings.
Receipts and Payments = real account of cash; Income and Expenditure = nominal account on accrual basis.
Legacies and specific donations are capital; general small donations are revenue.
Opening Capital Fund = Opening assets - Opening liabilities (special funds are liabilities).

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a Receipts and Payments Account and an Income and Expenditure Account.
questions.answer:
- **Nature**: R&P is a real account (summary of cash and bank); I&E is a nominal account like P&L.
- **Basis**: R&P is on cash basis; I&E is on accrual basis.
- **Items**: R&P includes capital and revenue receipts and payments of past, current and future years; I&E includes only revenue items relating to the current year.
- **Non-cash items**: depreciation, outstanding and prepaid items appear in I&E, never in R&P.
- **Balance**: R&P opens and closes with cash/bank balance (closing balance is always debit or nil); I&E closes with a surplus or deficit transferred to the Capital Fund.
- **Side**: receipts on the debit side of R&P; incomes on the credit side of I&E.

chapters.title: Partnership Accounts: Goodwill, Admission, Retirement, Death and Dissolution
chapters.summary: Appropriation of profits, valuation and treatment of goodwill, reconstitution of a firm on admission, retirement or death, and dissolution through the Realisation Account.
chapters.lawAsOf: Indian Partnership Act, 1932 (sections 13, 37 and 48); AS 26 Intangible Assets

lesson.heading: Partnership deed, appropriation and capital accounts
lesson.body:
Partners' rights are governed by the **partnership deed**. Where the deed is silent, section 13 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 applies:

| Matter | Rule in absence of agreement |
| --- | --- |
| Profit sharing | Equal |
| Interest on capital | Not allowed |
| Interest on drawings | Not charged |
| Salary or commission to partners | Not allowed |
| Interest on partner's loan or advance | 6% p.a., payable even if there is a loss |

The **Profit and Loss Appropriation Account** distributes net profit: interest on capital, salaries and commission are debited; interest on drawings is credited; the balance is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

- **Fixed capital**: capital accounts show only capital; all adjustments go to Current Accounts.
- **Fluctuating capital**: all adjustments go directly to capital accounts.

**Interest on drawings** (equal monthly drawings, 12 months): beginning of each month - average period 6.5 months; middle - 6 months; end - 5.5 months.

lesson.heading: Goodwill
lesson.body:
Goodwill is the value of a firm's reputation and its ability to earn more than normal profits. Methods:

- **Average profit**: Goodwill = Average profit x Number of years' purchase.
- **Super profit**: Super profit = Average profit - Normal profit (Capital employed x Normal rate). Goodwill = Super profit x Years' purchase.
- **Capitalisation of super profit**: Super profit x 100 / Normal rate.
- **Capitalisation of average profit**: (Average profit x 100 / Normal rate) - Capital employed.

Under **AS 26**, internally generated goodwill is not recognised as an asset. So on reconstitution, goodwill is **not raised in the books**; instead it is adjusted through partners' capital accounts. The incoming partner's share of goodwill (brought in cash as premium or debited to his capital) is credited to the sacrificing partners in the **sacrificing ratio**. Existing goodwill in the books is written off to old partners in the old ratio.

lesson.heading: Admission, retirement and death
lesson.body:
| Step | Admission | Retirement / death |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ratio | New ratio; sacrificing ratio = Old - New | Gaining ratio = New - Old |
| Goodwill | New partner's share credited to sacrificing partners | Outgoing partner's share debited to gaining partners |
| Revaluation | Gain or loss to old partners in old ratio | Gain or loss to all partners in old ratio |
| Reserves and accumulated profits | To old partners in old ratio | To all partners in old ratio |
| Settlement | Capital brought in | Amount due paid or transferred to loan account |

**Death**: the deceased partner's share of profit from the last balance sheet date to the date of death is calculated on the basis of last year's profit, average profit or sales, and debited to P&L Suspense (or gaining partners).

**Section 37**: if the firm continues to use an outgoing or deceased partner's share without final settlement, his estate may claim, at its option, either the share of profits earned with that money or interest at 6% p.a. on it.

lesson.heading: Dissolution
lesson.body:
On dissolution all assets (except cash, bank and fictitious assets) and outside liabilities are closed through the **Realisation Account**:

- Debit: assets at book value, payment of liabilities, realisation expenses (if borne by the firm).
- Credit: outside liabilities at book value, cash from assets, assets taken over by partners.
- Balance (profit or loss) to partners in the profit-sharing ratio.

**Section 48** order of settlement: losses (including deficiency of capital) are paid first out of profits, then out of capital, and lastly by partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio. Assets are applied: (a) to pay third-party debts, (b) to repay partners' loans and advances rateably, (c) to repay capital rateably, (d) any surplus divided in the profit-sharing ratio.

**Common mistakes**: crediting goodwill premium in the new ratio instead of the sacrificing ratio; raising goodwill in the books contrary to AS 26; passing partners' loans through Realisation Account (they are paid directly after outsiders).

keyPoints: No deed: equal profits, no interest on capital, no salary, 6% interest on partner's loan.
Sacrificing ratio = Old - New (admission); Gaining ratio = New - Old (retirement/death).
AS 26: self-generated goodwill is not recorded; adjust through capital accounts.
Interest on drawings at beginning of each month for 12 months: average 6.5 months.
Section 37: estate of outgoing partner may claim share of profits or 6% p.a. interest.
Section 48 order: outside debts, partners' loans, capital, then surplus in profit-sharing ratio.

cases.title: Case: Anand and Bose admit Chopra
cases.body:
**Anand** and **Bose** are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3:2. On 1 April 2027 they admit **Chopra** for a 1/5th share in future profits, which he acquires from Anand and Bose in their existing ratio.

- Chopra brings ₹2,00,000 as capital and his share of goodwill in cash.
- Goodwill is valued at 2 years' purchase of the average profits of the last 3 years: ₹1,80,000, ₹2,10,000 and ₹2,40,000.
- Building is revalued upward by ₹60,000; a provision for doubtful debts of ₹8,000 is created; stock is reduced by ₹12,000.
- The firm has no goodwill in its books. Capitals are fluctuating.

Sacrificing ratio = old ratio 3:2 (share taken in the old ratio). Anand gets 84,000 x 3/5 = **₹50,400**; Bose gets ₹33,600.

questions.prompt: In the absence of a partnership deed, a partner who has advanced a loan to the firm is entitled to interest at:
questions.explanation: Section 13(d) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 provides interest at 6% p.a. on advances by a partner beyond agreed capital. It is a charge against profit, payable even in a loss year.

questions.prompt: When a partner retires, the remaining partners compensate him for goodwill in the:
questions.explanation: The continuing partners gain the retiring partner's share, so they bear his share of goodwill in the gaining ratio (New - Old).

questions.prompt: On dissolution, a partner's loan to the firm is:
options: Paid after outside creditors and before partners' capitals
Paid only after capitals are returned
Transferred to the partner's capital account
questions.explanation: Under section 48, assets are applied first to third-party debts, then to partners' advances (loans), then to capital. The loan is not passed through Realisation Account.

questions.prompt: Under AS 26, a firm should raise a Goodwill Account for its self-generated goodwill on admission of a new partner.
questions.explanation: AS 26 does not allow recognition of internally generated goodwill. Only purchased goodwill is recorded; on admission the adjustment is made through partners' capital accounts.

questions.prompt: Select all items that are debited to Realisation Account on dissolution.
options: Realisation expenses paid by the firm
Cash realised from sale of stock
questions.explanation: Assets transferred at book value, payments to outside liabilities and realisation expenses borne by the firm are debits. Creditors at book value and cash realised are credits; partners' loans are settled outside Realisation Account.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: on retirement of a partner, the ratio in which the continuing partners acquire his share is called the ___ ratio.
questions.explanation: Gaining ratio = New ratio - Old ratio for each continuing partner.

questions.prompt: A partner withdrew ₹10,000 at the beginning of every month during 2026-27. Interest on drawings is 9% p.a. Compute the interest on drawings (in ₹).

chapters.title: Introduction to Company Accounts: Shares and Debentures
chapters.summary: Share capital, issue of shares at par and premium, over-subscription, calls in arrears and advance, forfeiture and reissue, and issue and redemption of debentures.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act, 2013 (sections 52, 53 and 71), Table F of Schedule I, and Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 as amended

lesson.heading: Share capital and issue of shares
lesson.body:
A company raises **share capital** from members. Categories shown in the notes to the Balance Sheet: **authorised** (maximum in the memorandum), **issued**, **subscribed**, **called-up** and **paid-up**. **Reserve capital** is the uncalled part that the company resolves to call only on winding up.

Shares may be issued at **par** or at a **premium**. Under **section 53**, a company cannot issue shares at a discount except sweat equity shares. Premium is credited to **Securities Premium Account**, which under **section 52(2)** may be used only for: issuing fully paid bonus shares; writing off preliminary expenses; writing off expenses, commission or discount on issue of shares or debentures; providing for premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures; and buy-back of own shares (section 68).

Entries for an issue payable in instalments:

| Event | Entry |
| --- | --- |
| Application money received | Bank Dr; To Share Application A/c |
| Transfer on allotment | Share Application Dr; To Share Capital (and Securities Premium if collected on application); To Share Allotment (excess adjusted); To Bank (refund) |
| Allotment due | Share Allotment Dr; To Share Capital (and Securities Premium if due on allotment) |
| Call due | Share Call Dr; To Share Capital |
| Money received | Bank Dr; To Share Allotment / Share Call |

**Over-subscription**: reject some applications (refund), allot pro rata (adjust excess towards allotment and calls), or a combination.

**Calls in arrears / in advance**: Table F allows interest on calls in arrears (up to 10% p.a.) and on calls in advance (up to 12% p.a.), unless the articles say otherwise.

lesson.heading: Forfeiture and reissue
lesson.body:
If a shareholder fails to pay an allotment or call, the directors may **forfeit** the shares as per the articles.

- Debit **Share Capital** with the amount called up on the forfeited shares.
- Debit **Securities Premium** only if the premium was due but **not received**.
- Credit the unpaid calls (or Calls in Arrears).
- Credit **Share Forfeiture Account** with the amount already received towards capital.

Forfeited shares may be **reissued**, even at a discount, but the discount cannot exceed the amount forfeited on those shares. On reissue: Bank Dr, Share Forfeiture Dr (discount); To Share Capital. The balance of forfeiture on the reissued shares is a capital profit and is transferred to **Capital Reserve**. Forfeiture relating to shares not yet reissued stays in Share Forfeiture Account (shown under share capital).

Worked example: 100 shares of ₹10 (₹8 called up, ₹6 paid) forfeited. Forfeiture: Share Capital Dr 800; To Calls in Arrears 200; To Share Forfeiture 600. All reissued at ₹7 as fully paid: Bank Dr 700, Share Forfeiture Dr 300; To Share Capital 1,000. Capital reserve = 600 - 300 = ₹300.

lesson.heading: Debentures: issue and redemption
lesson.body:
A **debenture** is an instrument acknowledging a debt; debentureholders are creditors who get fixed interest, whether or not there are profits.

| Terms | Entry on allotment (₹100 debenture) |
| --- | --- |
| Issue at par, redeemable at par | Bank Dr 100; To Debentures 100 |
| Issue at 5% discount, redeemable at par | Bank Dr 95, Discount on Issue Dr 5; To Debentures 100 |
| Issue at par, redeemable at 10% premium | Bank Dr 100, Loss on Issue Dr 10; To Debentures 100, To Premium on Redemption 10 |
| Issue at 5% discount, redeemable at 10% premium | Bank Dr 95, Loss on Issue Dr 15; To Debentures 100, To Premium on Redemption 10 |

Discount or loss on issue is written off (first against Securities Premium if available, else to P&L) over the life of the debentures. Debentures may also be issued as collateral security or for purchase of assets.

**Redemption**: in a lump sum, by instalments, by purchase in the open market, or by conversion. Section 71 and Rule 18(7) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 require certain companies to create a **Debenture Redemption Reserve** out of profits (for example, unlisted companies other than specified financial companies: 10% of outstanding debentures) and to invest or deposit a specified percentage of debentures maturing in the next year. The exact requirement depends on the class of company; check the current rule. DRR entry: Profit and Loss (Surplus) Dr; To DRR. After redemption, DRR is transferred to General Reserve.

**Common mistakes**: debiting Securities Premium on forfeiture when the premium was already received; allowing reissue discount above the forfeited amount; treating debentures as part of share capital.

keyPoints: Section 53: no issue of shares at a discount (except sweat equity).
Section 52(2): five permitted uses of Securities Premium; not for dividend.
Forfeiture: debit capital called up; debit premium only if not received; credit forfeiture with amount received on capital.
Max discount on reissue = amount forfeited on those shares; surplus on reissued shares to Capital Reserve.
Loss on issue of debentures = discount on issue + premium on redemption.
Table F: interest on calls in arrears up to 10%, on calls in advance up to 12% p.a. (unless articles provide otherwise).

cases.title: Case: Pinewood Ltd
cases.body:
**Pinewood Ltd** offered 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, payable:

| Instalment | ₹ per share |
| --- | --- |
| On application (including premium ₹2) | 5 |
| On allotment | 3 |
| On first and final call | 4 |

Applications were received for 70,000 shares. Applications for 10,000 shares were rejected and their money refunded. The remaining applicants were allotted shares **pro rata**, and excess application money was adjusted towards allotment.

**Rohan**, who was allotted 600 shares, failed to pay the allotment and the call. His shares were forfeited after the call. Later, 400 of these shares were reissued to Sana at ₹8 per share as fully paid.

questions.prompt: How much cash did Pinewood Ltd receive on allotment (in ₹)?
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Allotment due (50,000 x ₹3) | 1,50,000 |
| Less: Excess application money adjusted (10,000 shares x ₹5) | (50,000) |
| Less: Rohan's unpaid allotment (600 x 3 - 600 excess) | (1,200) |
| **Cash received on allotment** | **98,800** |

Pro-rata ratio 60,000 : 50,000 = 6:5. Rohan applied for 720 shares and paid ₹3,600; ₹600 (120 x 5) was adjusted towards his allotment.

questions.prompt: What amount is credited to Share Forfeiture Account on forfeiture of Rohan's shares (in ₹)?
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Share Capital A/c (600 x ₹10) | 6,000 |  |
| To Share Allotment A/c (unpaid) |  | 1,200 |
| To Share First and Final Call A/c (600 x 4) |  | 2,400 |
| To Share Forfeiture A/c |  | **2,400** |

Forfeited amount = what Rohan paid towards capital: 600 x ₹3 on application + ₹600 excess adjusted to allotment = ₹2,400. His ₹1,200 premium was received with the application and stays in Securities Premium.

questions.prompt: On forfeiture of Rohan's shares, Securities Premium Account is:
options: Not debited, because the premium was received with the application
questions.explanation: Securities Premium is reversed on forfeiture only when the premium was due but not received. Here it was payable and paid with the application, so it remains in the books.

questions.prompt: How much is transferred to Capital Reserve after the reissue of 400 shares (in ₹)?
questions.explanation: Forfeited amount on 400 shares = 2,400 x 400/600 = ₹1,600. Discount on reissue = 400 x (10 - 8) = ₹800. Capital reserve = 1,600 - 800 = **₹800**. The forfeiture of ₹800 on the 200 shares not reissued stays in Share Forfeiture Account.

questions.prompt: Pass the journal entries for forfeiture of Rohan's shares and their partial reissue.
questions.answer:
| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equity share capital A/c Dr | 6,000 |  |
| To Equity share allotment A/c |  | 1,200 |
| To Equity share first and final call A/c |  | 2,400 |
| To Share forfeiture A/c |  | 2,400 |
| (Being forfeiture of 600 shares for non-payment of allotment and call) |  |  |
| Bank A/c Dr | 3,200 |  |
| Share forfeiture A/c Dr | 800 |  |
| To Equity share capital A/c |  | 4,000 |
| (Being reissue of 400 forfeited shares at ₹8 as fully paid) |  |  |
| Share forfeiture A/c Dr | 800 |  |
| To Capital reserve A/c |  | 800 |
| (Being profit on reissue of 400 shares transferred) |  |  |

Balance in Share Forfeiture Account ₹800 (on 200 shares) is added to paid-up capital in the notes until those shares are reissued.

questions.prompt: Under section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company may issue shares at a discount only in the case of:
questions.explanation: Section 53 prohibits issue of shares at a discount, with an exception for sweat equity shares issued under section 54 (and certain conversions of debt under specified schemes).

questions.prompt: Securities Premium Account can NOT be used for:
options: Providing for premium payable on redemption of debentures
questions.explanation: Section 52(2) lists the permitted uses; payment of dividend is not one of them. Securities premium is treated like paid-up capital.

questions.prompt: 100 shares of ₹10 each, ₹7 called up and ₹4 paid, are forfeited and reissued as fully paid. The maximum discount allowed on reissue is:
questions.explanation: The forfeited amount is ₹400 (100 x ₹4 received). Discount on reissue cannot exceed it, so the shares must be reissued for at least ₹600 in total.

questions.prompt: Debentureholders are owners of the company and are entitled to vote at general meetings.
questions.explanation: Debentureholders are creditors. They receive fixed interest and repayment of principal and normally have no voting rights, unlike shareholders.

questions.prompt: Select all purposes for which Securities Premium may be applied under section 52(2).
options: Writing off discount on issue of debentures
Issue of fully paid bonus shares
Writing off losses on sale of fixed assets
questions.explanation: Section 52(2) allows bonus shares, preliminary expenses, expenses/commission/discount on issue of shares or debentures, premium on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buy-back. Operating or capital losses cannot be written off against it.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the portion of uncalled capital that a company resolves to call up only in the event of its winding up is called ___ capital.
questions.explanation: Reserve capital, created by special resolution, is available only to creditors on winding up. It differs from capital reserve, which is a capital profit.

questions.prompt: A company issued 10,000, 9% debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 5%, redeemable at a premium of 10%. Compute the loss on issue of debentures (in ₹).
questions.explanation:
Per debenture: discount ₹5 + premium on redemption ₹10 = ₹15. Total = 10,000 x 15 = **₹1,50,000**.

Entry: Bank Dr 9,50,000; Loss on Issue of Debentures Dr 1,50,000; To 9% Debentures 10,00,000; To Premium on Redemption of Debentures 1,00,000.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between shares and debentures.
questions.answer:
- **Status**: shareholders are owners (members); debentureholders are creditors.
- **Return**: dividend depends on profits and is declared at the board's or members' discretion; debenture interest is a fixed charge payable even in a loss year.
- **Voting**: equity shareholders vote; debentureholders normally do not.
- **Repayment**: share capital is not repaid during the company's life (except redeemable preference shares or buy-back); debentures are redeemed as per terms.
- **Security**: shares are unsecured; debentures are usually secured by a charge on assets.
- **Issue at discount**: shares cannot be issued at a discount (section 53, except sweat equity); debentures can.
- **Winding up**: debentureholders are paid before shareholders.
